narrative:
The model predicted a 54% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. First, your performance in the third year of law school was the strongest influence. Your decile ranking of 5.0 placed you below the average of accepted students (5.79), pulling the prediction toward failure. Second, your LSAT score of 23 was substantially lower than the 37.18 average among accepted applicants; this was the second-biggest factor and strongly pushed the model to expect you would not pass the bar. Third, your undergraduate GPA of 2.3, compared with an average of 3.23 for accepted students, added further weight toward predicting failure.

Although your upper-middle family income and full-time study plans aligned with the majority of successful applicants, they could not offset the combined impact of your academic indicators.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your law school grades in the remaining years, consider retaking the LSAT to boost your score, and explore bar-preparation resources early. Strengthening these areas will directly address the factors that led to the rejection. (218 words)
